title: The Grandfather Paradox
summary: If you travelled back in time and prevented your grandparents from meeting, you would never be born, so you could never travel back to prevent it. The puzzle is often traced to René Barjavel's novel Le Voyageur imprudent (1943), though pulp stories had played with the idea before, and it became a standard objection to the very possibility of time travel. In "The Paradoxes of Time Travel" (1976), David Lewis argued that the traveller Tim can, in one sense, kill his grandfather, and in another sense cannot, and both are true: he will fail for some commonplace reason, because the past already happened the way it did. Two families of replies followed: self-consistency (the past can only ever be the way it was: the physicist Igor Novikov's principle), and branching timelines (a change creates a different history, so there is no contradiction: David Deutsch's quantum version).
citations: David Lewis, "The Paradoxes of Time Travel," American Philosophical Quarterly 13 (1976): 145–152
Nicholas J. J. Smith, "Time Travel," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/time-travel/
